articles.title: The Demolition That Left Everything Else Standing
articles.dek: When a sixty-seven-year-old Las Vegas hotel fell in twenty seconds without cracking a window next door, it showed what Paul meant by a war fought with a different kind of weapon.
articles.quote: The weapon of heaven was never a wrecking ball. It is precise enough to bring down a lie and leave the person standing.
articles.body:
Before dawn on October 9, 2024, thousands of people lined the Las Vegas Strip and climbed onto hotel balconies, coffee in hand, phones raised, waiting for a countdown. The target was the Tropicana, a hotel that had stood for sixty-seven years and outlived a dozen versions of the city around it. In under twenty seconds, its two towers were gone, folded straight down into their own footprint in a controlled cascade of dust. What made the moment remarkable wasn't the size of the blast. It was the restraint. Every other building on that block, packed shoulder to shoulder with the Tropicana for decades, never so much as trembled.

That kind of precision takes months to earn. Demolition engineers spend that time studying blueprints, identifying the handful of support columns actually carrying the building's weight, and packing charges only there. Then comes the harder part: sequencing hundreds of individual detonations down to fractions of a second, so the structure collapses inward and downward instead of toppling out into the street. A wrecking ball would have taken weeks and cracked windows for blocks. A careless charge would have taken the neighbors down with it. What actually happened was surgical. Only the condemned structure fell. Everything beside it kept standing.

Paul had something like that in mind when he sat down to answer his critics in Corinth. By the time he wrote this letter, some in that church had started listening to voices louder than his — confident speakers who told the Corinthians that Paul, in person, was unimpressive next to them. So Paul opens by naming exactly how he plans to answer: not with their kind of noise, but with "the humility and gentleness of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:1). Then, in the very next breath, he makes sure no one mistakes that gentleness for softness.

"For though we live in the world, we do not wage war as the world does," he writes. "The weapons we fight with are not the weapons of the world. On the contrary, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. We demolish arguments and every pretension that sets itself up against the knowledge of God, and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ."

2 Corinthians 10:3–5

Read that again slowly, and notice what it does not say. It doesn't say we demolish people. It doesn't say we tear down our opponents, or flatten a reputation, or win by outshouting the loudest voice in the room. It says we demolish arguments. Pretensions. Thoughts that have set themselves up like little fortresses against the knowledge of God. The target is specific. It is the lie, not the person carrying it.

That's the detail I'd never noticed before. Worldly warfare — the kind Paul's critics were using, and the kind most of us default to without thinking — tends to work like a wrecking ball. It's loud, it's broad, and it damages whatever stands nearby. Say the wrong word in an argument and you don't just knock down someone's bad idea, you knock down their dignity with it. Turn that same ball inward, on yourself, and it's worse: one bad decision becomes "I always ruin everything." One failure becomes "I'm not the kind of person who succeeds." The stronghold and the person get flattened together, because the demolition was never aimed. The weapon of heaven was never a wrecking ball. It is precise enough to bring down a lie and leave the person standing.

A few verses later Paul makes the purpose explicit: his authority, he says, was given "for building you up rather than pulling you down" (2 Corinthians 10:8). Even the tearing down exists to serve the building up. That's not the logic of a wrecking ball. That's the logic of an engineer who studies the blueprint first, so that what falls is only what was never meant to keep standing.

So what does this actually look like on a Tuesday?

Start by finding the lie that's load-bearing. Not every worry deserves a full campaign — most collapse on their own soon enough. But there's usually one belief sitting where a support column should be: God can't really forgive what I did. I'll always be the disappointment in this family. Prayer doesn't change anything, so why bother. That's the pretension Paul means — not a stray thought, but one holding up a whole way of seeing yourself or God.

Then use the right charge, placed in the right spot. Scripture that speaks directly to that lie, rather than general encouragement. An honest conversation with someone who will tell you the truth in love instead of piling on. Prayer that names the actual argument instead of a vague unease. None of these are loud weapons. They rarely make a scene. But aimed precisely, they can bring down in a season what shouting at yourself never touched in years.

And when it falls, notice who is left standing. You are. Not flattened alongside the lie, but free of it — the way the Tropicana's neighbors woke up the next morning exactly where they had always been, one building lighter on the block.

Paul was never the loudest voice in Corinth, and by his own account he never tried to be. But he trusted a different kind of power — gentle enough to appeal, and precise enough to tear down only what was never supposed to be standing in the first place. Carry that into whatever argument or old accusation you're facing this week, whether it's aimed at you or coming from inside your own head. Find the load-bearing lie. Bring the precise weapon, not the wrecking ball. And let it fall. You were never the target. Only the lie was.

articles.title: The Enemy God Called "My People"
articles.dek: Isaiah looked at Israel's two most feared enemies and pictured a future where God called them by his own family names — no asterisks, no fine print.
articles.quote: The God who could have kept blessing for Israel alone built a highway instead, and called yesterday's enemies by name: my people, my handiwork, my inheritance.
articles.body:
In 2012, researchers at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center went looking for something strange: male DNA inside the brains of women who had died of ordinary causes. These weren't women who'd had transplants or transfusions. They were mothers. And decades after giving birth to sons, most of them were still quietly carrying their children's cells, folded into their own brain tissue as if the cells had always belonged there. Scientists call it fetal microchimerism. Nobody expected it to last a lifetime.

During pregnancy, a small number of the baby's cells slip across the placenta into the mother's bloodstream. By every rule of immunology, her body should treat them as foreign invaders and destroy them, the way it would a transplanted organ from a stranger. Instead, something gentler happens. The cells are welcomed in. They migrate. They settle in the brain, the heart, the thyroid, the skin. In several studies, researchers have found these fetal cells clustered thickest at the exact site of a mother's later illness — heart tissue after a cardiac injury, a scar after surgery — as if they had shown up specifically to help her heal. Difference didn't disqualify them. It just changed what they were used for.

Isaiah never studied a placenta, but centuries before any of this had a name, he wrote about a mercy shaped just like it. In Isaiah 19, the prophet turns his attention to Egypt, and at first it is nothing but bad news. Egypt's idols totter, its rivers dry up, its economy collapses, its counselors give foolish advice, and the nation turns on itself in civil war. This is not a random target. Egypt was the house of Israel's four hundred years of slavery, the empire whose Pharaoh had to be begged, plagued, and drowned in the Red Sea before he would let God's people go. Assyria, named right alongside Egypt, was worse still — the empire that would soon march into the northern kingdom, tear it apart, and scatter its people so completely that history calls them the Ten Lost Tribes. These are not neutral nations in Isaiah's world. They are the two great terrors of Israel's national memory, the names a Hebrew mother might have used to frighten a child into finishing dinner.

Then, without warning, the prophecy turns. Five times Isaiah repeats the phrase "in that day," and each time the picture softens. Egypt builds an altar to the Lord. God sends Egypt a savior and a defender. Egypt and Assyria stop fighting each other and start worshiping together. A highway opens between the two empires, and their people travel back and forth freely, as neighbors instead of invaders. Israel, the nation that had every reason to expect first place, is folded into the picture as a third partner — not a ruler over the other two, just one more guest at the same table.

"In that day Israel will be the third, along with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing on the earth. The Lord Almighty will bless them, saying, 'Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria my handiwork, and Israel my inheritance.'" (Isaiah 19:24–25, NIV)

Read that line slowly and something remarkable surfaces. "My people" is the phrase God thundered through Moses at the burning bush and at Pharaoh's gate: "Let my people go." Back then, the words were aimed at Pharaoh, but they were never about Pharaoh's nation — they were about someone else's freedom. Now, generations later, God speaks the identical words directly over Egypt itself. The nation that once refused to release God's people is, without qualification, called God's people. Assyria receives its own tender title, "my handiwork," the same kind of language Isaiah later uses for Israel's own children, calling them "the work of my hands" (Isaiah 29:23). Notice what's missing: no ranking, no probation period, no smaller print for the latecomers. Egypt and Assyria aren't tolerated additions bolted onto Israel's blessing. They're named in the same breath, with the same warmth, as the chosen people themselves.

This is what makes the fetal cell discovery such an apt mirror. The mother's body doesn't pretend those cells came from nowhere — they are still, genetically, her child's, still marked as other. But her body stops treating that difference as a threat to be managed and starts treating it as family to be housed, protected, and even leaned on in a crisis. The origin isn't erased. It's just no longer the basis for exclusion. That is precisely the move Isaiah describes: God does not ask Egypt to stop being Egypt, or Assyria to stop being Assyria, in order to belong. He simply refuses to let their long history of enmity be the final word on who gets to sit at his table.

Most of us are carrying a version of Egypt or Assyria in our own lives — a relative who wronged us, an in-law we've stopped inviting, a former friend whose name still tightens something in our chest. Filipino families know this particular ache well: the cousins who haven't spoken since a land dispute, the tita who was never forgiven for something said at a wake. Isaiah's vision isn't a call to pretend the wound never happened; Egypt's judgment in this same chapter is real and severe. But it is an invitation to imagine a highway where you've only ever built a wall. That might look small this week — a message sent to someone you wrote off years ago, a seat left open at your table, a willingness to let a former rival's good news please you instead of threaten you. Highways get built one plank at a time, and Isaiah insists God is already laying the road, long before either side has fully earned it.

The God who could have kept blessing for Israel alone built a highway instead, and called yesterday's enemies by name: my people, my handiwork, my inheritance. If he can say that over Egypt and Assyria, he can say it over whoever's name you've been avoiding this year. Maybe this week, quietly, you let him — and you build one plank toward them yourself.

articles.title: The Father Who Remembered the Clay
articles.dek: Before he calls us dust, God remembers exactly how he shaped it — and that changes everything about how he treats our limits.
articles.quote: He doesn't measure you against anyone else's frame — only the exact one he shaped you from.
articles.body:
On November 7, 2020, at Ironman Florida in Panama City Beach, a young man named Chris Nikic crossed a finish line with fourteen minutes to spare before the seventeen-hour cutoff. Behind him lay a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike ride, and a 26.2-mile marathon, all completed in a single day. Chris has Down syndrome. He became the first person with that diagnosis ever to finish a full Ironman triathlon.

The headline was the finish line. The real story was his father. Nik Nikic, a corporate executive, had spent years building the training plan that got his son there, and the plan rested on one unusual decision. He never asked Chris to move, balance, or recover the way other athletes did. Down syndrome affects muscle tone and motor planning in ways that make standard coaching cues useless — the ordinary drills simply don't fit that body. So instead of measuring Chris against a generic standard, Nik studied exactly how his son was made: the way his balance worked, the extra seconds he needed transitioning from swim to bike, the particular rhythm his legs could hold on a run. He built the whole plan around that one body, not an average one. Their shared phrase, repeated for years before it ever became a headline, was simple: one percent better today. Not "match the field." Just better than yesterday, by the measure of what today's body could actually give.

That is the kind of compassion Psalm 103 is describing — and it is easy to read past it, because the psalm sounds, at first, like general praise. David opens by blessing the Lord for forgiving sin, healing disease, redeeming life from the pit. He widens the lens: the Lord made his ways known to Moses, is compassionate and gracious, does not treat us as our sins deserve, removes our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west. It reads like a hymn about God in general — vast, cosmic, sung over the whole of humanity.

Then, right in the middle of that vastness, David narrows the lens all the way down to one relationship, one image, one kind of love that anyone who has ever raised a child would recognize instantly.

"As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him; for he knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust." (Psalm 103:13–14, NIV)

Here is what is easy to miss on a first reading: that word "formed" is not decoration. In Hebrew it's the same verb, yatsar, used back in Genesis for a potter shaping clay — the very word used when the Lord formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed life into him. David isn't saying God has generic sympathy for fragile creatures in general. He's saying God remembers, specifically, the shaping. The exact hands-on work of making you the way you are — your particular limits, your particular pace, your particular breaking points — is not new information to him. He was there when the clay was still wet.

That changes what "he remembers that we are dust" actually means. It isn't God sighing at how disappointing we are. It's a father recalling, with tenderness, precisely what material he was working with when he made you — the way Nik Nikic knew, better than any generic coach ever could, exactly what Chris's particular body needed and did not need. A coach who trained Chris like every other triathlete would have quit on him, or broken him, within a month. Compassion that isn't tailored to how someone is actually made isn't really compassion — it's just an average, applied to a person who was never average to begin with.

Most of us carry around a quiet, exhausting habit of comparing our dust to someone else's. We measure our prayer life against a friend's, our patience against a parent's, our faith against the composed-looking person three pews over, and we come away feeling like defective material. But that comparison was never the standard David describes. The Father who has compassion "on those who fear him" is not grading on a curve set by your neighbor's formation. He is grading — if grading is even the right word — against the one thing he actually knows in full: exactly how he shaped you, and exactly what you're carrying today.

The psalm doesn't stop at tenderness, either. A few lines later it turns almost startlingly honest about how little our days amount to: "the life of mortals is like grass, they flourish like a flower of the field; the wind blows over it and it is gone" (Psalm 103:15–16). That's not despair. It's the same logic as the potter line, said out loud. Our days are short and our strength is limited — he already knew that when he formed us. The fragility isn't a surprise he's disappointed to discover. It's the very thing his compassion was built to meet, "from everlasting to everlasting" (v. 17), long before the flower ever opened and long after the wind has carried it off.

It's worth asking, honestly, what you've been quietly demanding of your own dust lately — some spiritual mile pace you assume you should be able to hold, some emotional recovery time you think you shouldn't need, some steadiness you've watched in someone else and quietly resented not having. Psalm 103 is not telling you to stop trying. It's telling you who you're actually training under, and what he already knows about the body and soul he gave you.

He doesn't measure you against anyone else's frame — only the exact one he shaped you from.

Chris Nikic still races. He's finished more Ironmans since that first one, each time a little faster, a little steadier, always chasing one percent, never chasing someone else's pace. His father never once asked him to move like the man in the next lane. He asked him to move like Chris — because that was the body, and the heart, he had actually come to know.

You are not being measured against the pace of the person praying beside you, working beside you, or grieving beside you. The one who formed you from dust remembers precisely what he put in and precisely what he left out, and his compassion was fitted to that shape before you ever took your first breath. Tonight, instead of asking whether you did enough today, try asking a smaller, kinder question: was it one percent more faithful than yesterday, given exactly what you were carrying? For a Father who remembers your dust that well, that may be exactly enough.

articles.title: The Fare That Passed Through Eight Hands
articles.dek: In a crowded jeepney, a twenty-peso bill travels farther than you'd think — and Proverbs 13 says something is riding along with it.
articles.quote: A trustworthy envoy doesn't just deliver a message. He brings healing.
articles.illustration: jeepney fare passed hand to hand
articles.body:
Squeeze onto a jeepney during rush hour in Manila, and you'll see a small miracle nobody applauds. A passenger in the back hands a twenty-peso bill forward. It passes through four hands, sometimes eight, all the way to the driver — strangers who never asked to be trusted, passing along money that isn't theirs. The driver counts it, makes change, and sends it back the same way, coin by coin, through the same chain of strangers. Nobody skims a peso off the top. Nobody pockets the change and pretends it got lost. It just arrives, all the way to the person waiting for it at the back. Multiply that by the thousands of jeepneys crossing Metro Manila every single day, with no contract, no camera, no supervisor watching, and you start to see how much quiet trust this country runs on without ever naming it. It works because for a few seconds, a stranger becomes your messenger — and almost always, they carry what's yours like it matters.

Solomon noticed the same quiet miracle three thousand years ago, and he built one of his sharpest proverbs on it. Proverbs 13 is a string of short, plainspoken contrasts — the kind of sayings a father repeats to his son so many times they become instinct. The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning a person from the snares of death, he says in verse 14. Good judgment wins favor, but the way of the unfaithful leads to their destruction, he says in verse 15. The prudent act with knowledge, but fools can't help exposing their folly — they blurt out what should stay quiet, he says in verse 16. And then, almost as an afterthought, tucked between sayings about wisdom and wealth, comes a proverb about something smaller: what happens when you send someone to carry your errand for you.

"A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a trustworthy envoy brings healing." (Proverbs 13:17, NIV)

Notice what Solomon doesn't say about the envoy. He doesn't say the trustworthy one is clever, fast, or impressive. He says exactly one thing: he can be trusted with what isn't his. The Hebrew word behind "trustworthy" here is aman — the same root behind our word amen. It means solid, dependable, load-bearing, the kind of word you could build a house on. The word behind "envoy" pictures someone sent to carry another person's business — an ambassador, a courier, a go-between. He didn't write the message. He didn't earn the money in his hand. He was simply given something for the length of an errand. And Solomon says that one small window of trust is enough to either wound something or heal it. It's worth noticing, too, that the word for what the trustworthy envoy brings — healing — echoes the "fountain of life" language back in verse 14. Wisdom that turns people from death, and faithfulness that heals what's broken, are cut from the same cloth. Even the fool in verse 16, who can't keep his mouth shut, is really a small-scale version of the wicked messenger — someone who was trusted with information and couldn't help but mishandle it.

Most of us will never carry a king's letter across a desert. But we carry smaller things every day that aren't ours to keep. A message a friend asked us to pass along exactly as she said it, not sharpened or softened to make ourselves look better in the telling. Money entrusted for a specific bill, or tucked into a balikbayan box for someone waiting overseas. A confidence someone handed us at their most vulnerable, maybe over merienda, maybe in a text message marked huwag mo sanang sabihin. A task a boss delegated, trusting we'd finish it the way they would have, not the way that's easiest for us. Each one is a twenty-peso bill passed into our hands in a crowded jeepney — small, easy to mishandle, and never really ours.

Filipino life is full of these small envoy moments beyond the jeepney too. Ask a door-to-door courier why families hand over a balikbayan box that took two years of overseas salary to fill, and he'll tell you it isn't the tape or the tracking number that earns that trust — it's a name passed along by referral, because he's carried a hundred boxes before and never once opened one. Ask why a probinsyano heading home for fiesta will hand-carry an envelope of pera padala for a neighbor's mother he's never met, and he'll shrug: sabi lang niya, ibigay mo lang. She just said, just give it to her. No promissory note. No signature. Just a word passed from one mouth to another's ear, and somehow, it holds.

This is where the gospel quietly stands behind Solomon's proverb. Jesus described his own mission in exactly these terms. "I have not spoken on my own," he said, "but the Father who sent me commanded me to say all that I have spoken" (John 12:49). He carried God's message to us across an infinite distance and delivered it whole — not one word added, not one softened to spare himself trouble, not one syllable lost along the way. He was the trustworthy envoy who brought, not just information, but healing itself, the kind Isaiah had promised when he wrote that by his wounds we are healed. And then Jesus turned to his followers and said, "As the Father has sent me, I am sending you" (John 20:21). We are handed something we didn't write and didn't earn — the news that we're loved and forgiven — and asked only to carry it faithfully to whoever is waiting at the back of the jeepney.

So here's a question worth sitting with today: what has been placed in your hands that belongs to someone else? A word to relay exactly as it was given. A peso to pass on in full. A trust to keep, even when no one would ever find out if you didn't. You don't have to be remarkable to carry any of it well. You just have to remember, for the few seconds it's in your grip, that it isn't yours to keep — only yours to carry.

Next time you're the one in the middle of a crowded jeepney, holding someone else's fare in your palm, let it remind you what you were made for. Not to hold onto what passes through your hands, but to carry it well, all the way home. Somewhere at the back, someone is waiting for exactly what was entrusted to you — no more, no less — and a trustworthy envoy doesn't just deliver a message. He brings healing.
